question.prompt: Let the letters \(F,\) \(L,\) \(Y,\) \(B,\) \(U,\) \(G\) represent distinct digits. Suppose \(\text{FLYFLY}\) is the greatest number that satisfies the equation \[ 8 \cdot \text{FLYFLY} = \text{BUGBUG}. \] What is the value of \(\text{FLY} + \text{BUG}?\)

solutions.explanation:
Repeating a three-digit block places one copy in the thousands and leaves one copy at the end. Let \(a\) be the three-digit number \(\text{FLY}\), and let \(b\) be the three-digit number \(\text{BUG}\). Then
\[
\text{FLYFLY}=1000a+a=1001a,
\]
and similarly \(\text{BUGBUG}=1001b\). The given equation becomes \(8\cdot1001a=1001b\). Dividing both sides by the nonzero number \(1001\) gives
\[
8a=b.
\]
Because \(b\) has three digits and \(8\cdot125=1000\), the integer \(a\) is at most \(124\). Also, maximizing \(1001a\) is the same as maximizing \(a\), since the multiplier \(1001\) is positive.

Start with the largest possible candidate. If \(a=124\), then \(b=992\), which repeats the digit \(9\) and violates the distinct-digit condition. The next candidate is \(a=123\), giving
\[
8\cdot123=984.
\]
The six digits \(1,2,3,9,8,4\) are all distinct, so this candidate is valid. It gives \(8\cdot123123=984984\), and every larger candidate has already been ruled out. Therefore
\[
\text{FLY}+\text{BUG}=123+984=\boxed{1107},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Reduce to three digits and check the largest candidates
